Photograph: GoFundMe Michigan Ex-safety manager given 19 months’ prison over five-year-old’s hyperbaric chamber fire death Jeffrey Mosteller pleaded no contest to charges relating to burning death of Thomas Cooper in Michigan Marina Dunbar Fri 4 Sep 2026 17.51 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 17.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A former safety manager has been sentenced to one year and seven months in prison in connection with the death of a five-year-old Michigan boy who was killed in a fiery January 2025 explosion inside a hyperbaric oxygen chamber. Jeffrey Mosteller, 66, received that sentence after pleading no contest to involuntary manslaughter in Oakland county circuit court in Michigan on Monday. He worked as the safety manager at the Oxford Center, an alternative healthcare facility that treats children with a range of health conditions – including autism, ADHD and autoimmune diseases – using hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Mosteller faced up to 15 years in prison before being handed his 19-month sentence. Five-year-old Thomas Cooper, of Royal Oak, Michigan, was undergoing treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and sleep apnea at the Oxford Center in the Detroit suburb of Troy when a fire erupted inside the hyperbaric chamber. That triggered an explosion which killed Cooper. According to an expert who viewed video of the case, the child had squirmed enough to pull the sheet off a mattress inside the chamber, causing a spark of static electricity. That spark became a flash fire that incinerated him within seconds because of the oxygen-rich environment surrounding him. Cooper’s mother was badly burned on her arms and chest while desperately trying to open the tank. Mosteller is one of four former Oxford Center employees charged in connection with Thomas’s death. The other three were still awaiting trial at the time of his sentence. The Oxford Center founder and chief executive, Tamela Peterson, 58, was charged with second-degree murder. Facility manager Gary Marken, 65, was charged with second-degree murder and involuntary manslaughter. And Aleta Moffitt, 60, who was operating the chamber when it exploded, was charged with involuntary manslaughter and intentionally placing false medical information on a medical records chart. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cleared hyperbaric chambers to be marketed as safe and effective for 13 disorders , including severe burns, decompression sickness and non-healing wounds. The therapy works by delivering pure oxygen to a person’s body inside a pressurized chamber. Despite its FDA approval in certain cases, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) has been a growing source of controversy as the safety of these chambers have been called into question. Many allies of Trump administration health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr have endorsed HBOT, but many others have expressed skepticism towards the treatment’s increasing push into the healthcare mainstream. Cooper’s parents filed a $100m wrongful death lawsuit against the clinic and the chamber’s manufacturer over their son’s death. Photograph: Gauthier Bedrignans/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images Global Briefing Denis Staunton's guide to understanding world events - what’s happening, why it matters and how it affects you Sign up Denis Staunton Thu Oct 08 2026 - 06:13 • 3 MIN READ The French school students whose demonstrations have been making headlines are part of a global stirring among young people tired of getting a raw deal from older generations who are often indifferent or contemptuous towards their concerns. A generation finds its voice The school protests that have been roiling France spread to Belgium this week when hundreds of students demonstrated in the eastern city of Liège in protest against rising costs, overcrowded classrooms and a shortage of study materials. Police detained more than 100 people but responded to the protests with less brutality than their French counterparts and the city’s mayor has called for dialogue with the students. The protests in France and Belgium are part of a wave of unrest among students around the world in recent months and the European Students’ Union monitored 54 protest actions across the continent between March and May this year. Fourteen of them involved multiple cities and campuses, including demonstrations in 50 Italian cities in May, and some protests have been going on for months or even years. READ MORE Welcome to the new Global Briefing newsletter Can an everyday Methodist pastor create a political miracle in Kansas? Trump’s backing fails to lift Netanyahu as Israel heads for defining vote Will French unrest benefit Marine Le Pen’s presidential run? The triggers behind the protests are various but most are driven by frustration linked to the material conditions of education and extra burdens imposed on students. They are acts of resistance by a generation that is tired of being either hectored and bullied or ignored and dismissed by a governing class that is often indifferent to the concerns of young people as it squanders their future. In Romania last month, students across the country went to school dressed in black in protest against a bill that would introduce mandatory school uniforms. The students argue that instead of policing their clothing, the government in Bucharest, which spends less on education than most European Union member-states, should address structural problems in the school system and get serious about tackling child poverty. Protesters clash with riot police during a demonstration against education spending cuts in Liège, Belgium on Wednesday. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA India’s Cockroach movement launched one of the most successful student protests in recent history when it forced the resignation of Narendra Modi’s education minister over leaked exam papers that saw more than two million people forced to re-sit a medical school entrance exam. The movement initiated fresh protests last week over changes to India’s electoral roll that have seen millions of people stripped of the franchise. Governments around the world have responded to student protests with violence which has in some cases led to the deaths of demonstrators. Abdoulaye Ba, a second-year dental student at Cheikh Anta Diop University in the Senegalese capital of Dakar, died last February of multiple internal haemorrhages after police entered a dormitory and attacked students with batons. The students had been demonstrating against the failure to pay the government stipends that are the only source of income for many, leaving them unable to afford food or rent. The university authorities suspended student associations and closed student housing and the cafeteria when students were unable to pay for meals and accommodation. In the EU, education’s share of government spending has been flat or falling in recent years despite the fact that more students are being encouraged to enter third-level institutions. The EU has a target for the proportion of 25-34 year-olds to reach 45 per cent by 2030 but the funding per student has been falling, something which might be contributing to weaker European performance in the PISA study of educational attainment. While education budgets are squeezed, European governments are borrowing hundreds of billions of euros to spend on defence and some EU member-states have reinstated national military service while others are considering it. This means that if their governments’ diplomatic incompetence leads to war, the generation that stayed at home during the pandemic to protect their elders will be better trained to go away and die for them.
